healthcareSystem: Universal (National Insurance Scheme — primarily for residents; tourists can access public healthcare at cost)
qualityNotes: Norway has an excellent, well-funded healthcare system. Primary care and specialist services are widely available. Hospitals in all major cities; smaller communities have health clinics. English is universally spoken by medical staff. Pharmacies (apotek) are well-stocked.
pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies open 9am-6pm Mon-Fri, 9am-4pm Sat; some late-night/24-hour pharmacies in major cities; chains include Apotek 1, Vitusapotek, and Boots
pharmacyTips: Many common OTC medications available. Pharmacists are helpful and knowledgeable. Some medications may require a Norwegian prescription. Bring all prescription medications you may need, especially when traveling to remote areas (Lofoten, Svalbard, inland).
prescriptionRules: A valid prescription (ideally from a Norwegian or EEA doctor) is required for prescription medications. EEA prescriptions may be recognized for EU/EEA citizens. Carry all medications in original packaging with a doctor's note.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD stimulant medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Stimulants are controlled substances (narcotics class A/B). Bring original prescription, doctor's letter, and only the amount needed. Declare at customs. May need a permit from the Norwegian Medicines Agency for larger quantities.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine is controlled. Some products may be available with prescription. Carry alternatives if possible.

restrictedMeds.name: Psychotropic medications (diazepam, alprazolam, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Benzodiazepines require documentation. Carry a doctor's letter explaining medical necessity.

bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in English listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry original prescriptions and a note explaining medical necessity. Given Norway's remote areas and expensive healthcare, bring adequate supplies of all medications.

travelInsurance.tips: Healthcare in Norway is very expensive for non-residents. A doctor visit costs $150-300+, specialist visits $250-500+, hospital stays $1,000-3,000+/day. Travel insurance with medical coverage is strongly recommended. Medical evacuation from remote areas (northern Norway, Svalbard, hiking trails) can cost $10,000-50,000+. Ensure coverage includes emergency medical evacuation.

recommended: Tick-borne encephalitis (for summer hiking in endemic areas)
vaccinations.notes: No required vaccinations for travelers from any country. COVID-19 requirements vary — check current entry requirements. Tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) is a risk for hikers in southern Norway during summer months. Ensure routine vaccinations are up to date.

waterNotes: Tap water is safe and of excellent quality throughout Norway. It comes from protected mountain sources and is among the cleanest in the world. Bottled water is unnecessary — bring a reusable bottle. Freshwater streams and lakes in pristine areas are generally safe to drink from.
foodSafetyTips: Norway has very high food safety standards. All food sold commercially is safe. Traditional Norwegian cuisine (seafood, reindeer, salmon) from restaurants is safe. Be cautious with self-caught fish in areas with environmental advisories. Food from grocery stores is safe.
medicalTourismNote: Norway is not a medical tourism destination. Healthcare is excellent but expensive and primarily serves residents. Minor procedures for international patients available at high costs. No significant medical tourism infrastructure.
metaDescription: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Norway. Emergency number (112/113), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, vaccination requirements, water safety, and travel insurance advice.
